scenarios.title: Scenario 1: Secure Data Storage Using AES
scenarios.context: A healthcare organization stores sensitive patient records in a database. AES protects data at rest, but encryption keys were stored on the same server as the data.

questions.q: 1. Explain how AES provides confidentiality for stored data.
questions.a: AES is a symmetric block cipher that turns plaintext into ciphertext with a secret key. Without that key an attacker sees random-looking blocks—not readable diagnoses or IDs.
points: Same key encrypts and decrypts (symmetric).
Confidentiality = hiding meaning behind ciphertext.
Fast enough for encrypting millions of rows.

questions.q: 2. Identify and explain three security weaknesses.
questions.a: (1) Keys beside data means stealing the server steals “lock + spare key”. (2) One admin compromise can grab both blobs and keystores—no segregation. (3) Snapshots/backups propagate the leaked key so history collapses.
points: Key/data co-location voids AES benefit.
Weak IAM expands who may touch secrets.
No KMS/HSM separation = single fatal breach surface.

questions.q: 3. Describe how an attacker could exploit poor key management.
questions.a: After exploiting SQL injection, RCE or a leaked backup ZIP the attacker dumps configs or keystores reads the AES master key offline and decrypts the whole database peacefully.
points: Keys extracted from repos, disks, snapshots, ENV files.
Once the key leaks bulk decryption is scripted.
The math of AES survives—storage discipline fails.

questions.q: 4. Propose a secure key management strategy.
questions.a: Use a KMS or HSM off the DB host encrypt data keys separately (envelope crypto) automate rotation MFA least privilege logging vault break glass dual control forbid pushing secrets via Git.
points: Keys never plaintext on DB servers.
Automate rotation deny-by-default IAM.
Separate duties for escrow / emergency decrypt.

questions.q: 5. Evaluate strengths and limitations of AES in this scenario.
questions.a: Strength: mature high-speed cipher ideal for resting records. Limitation: AES secrecy depends entirely on key hygiene—lost keys ruin confidentiality instantly.
points: Algorithm strong governance decides outcome.
Symmetric means every copy matters equally.
Add integrity/signing separately if tampering risks matter.

scenarios.title: Scenario 4: AES Implementation Vulnerability
scenarios.context: An application uses AES in ECB mode to encrypt sensitive files.

questions.a: AES encrypts fixed 128-bit blocks with keyed rounds of substitution and mixing. The maths is approved for strength, yet how you glue blocks together (cipher mode + IV/nonces + integrity) decides whether real systems stay safe.
points: AES is a symmetric block cipher.
Supports 128/192/256-bit keys.
Mode misuse can leak patterns even though AES cores stay strong.

questions.q: 2. Describe why ECB mode is insecure.
questions.a: ECB repeats the same ciphertext for identical plaintext blocks, so striped images leak outlines and patterned records leak structure. Attackers can cut, reorder and replay ciphertext without knowing the AES key.
points: Repeated blocks → repeated ciphertext fragments.
Enables ciphertext editing / replay tricks.
Unsuitable whenever structure matters (files, spreadsheets, BMPs).

questions.q: 3. Identify patterns that may leak through ECB encryption.
questions.a: Logos, spreadsheets with repeated cells, BMP headers, barcode-like bitmaps or fixed-column DB rows—all create identical plaintext blocks revealing equal ciphertext blobs an adversary fingerprints.
points: Bitmap QR codes suffer worst visibly.
Database fixed-width repeating values align into blocks.
Compressed templates amplify repeating tokens.

questions.q: 4. Recommend a more secure mode (CBC GCM) and justify.
questions.a: Use AES-GCM (AEAD) so each ciphertext both conceals tampering triggers tag failures on alteration and runs fast on CPUs with AES-NI. CBC plus HMAC can work legacy but fragile ordering pitfalls vs single AEAD primitive.
points: GCM is today’s mainstream AEAD defaults.
Random IV + unique nonce pairing mandatory—reuse breaks everything.
CBC+HMAC viable only with random IV/HMAC-done-right discipline.

points: IV usually public yet unpredictable uniqueness critical.

mock.title: Q1 — Fake Antivirus at the Bank
mock.context: A bank employee unknowingly installs a fake antivirus software. Soon after, customer accounts begin to show unauthorized access and fraudulent transactions.

questions.q: (a) Identify the type of malware involved and explain how it works.
questions.a: It is a Trojan Horse (a fake-AV / rogueware Trojan). The user is tricked into running it because it looks like real antivirus software. Once installed, it secretly drops a keylogger and a banking infostealer that capture login details and send them to the attacker, who then logs into customer accounts and moves money.
points: Type = Trojan Horse (fake antivirus / rogueware).
Spreads by social engineering, not self-replication.
Drops keylogger + credential stealer + backdoor.
Stolen logins are sent to a Command-and-Control (C2) server.
Attacker uses them for Account Take-Over fraud.

questions.q: (b) What are indicators of malware infection the IT team should monitor?
questions.a: The team should watch for unusual host and network behaviour: high CPU when the PC is idle, unknown processes, disabled antivirus, new auto-start entries, and strange outbound traffic. On the bank side, watch for fraudulent transactions, logins from new countries and impossible-travel events.
points: Host: high CPU at idle, unknown processes, disabled AV, new startup entries.
Network: beaconing, unusual DNS, large outbound transfers.
Banking: unauthorised transfers, foreign logins, password-reset spam.
User experience: pop-ups, browser redirects, slow PC.
Centralise alerts in a SIEM and follow the IR plan.

questions.q: (c) Describe how Rootkits and Trojans differ and how each can be detected and removed.
questions.a: A Trojan tricks the user and runs at user level — easy to spot and usually removed by AV. A Rootkit hides deep in the OS kernel or boot sector to stay invisible, so normal AV often misses it. In a bank, Trojans are cleaned with EDR/AV, but rootkit-infected machines should be wiped and rebuilt from a clean image and all credentials rotated.
points: Trojan = user-level, deception-based, easy to detect.
Rootkit = kernel/boot-level, hides itself, very hard to detect.
Detect Trojans with AV/EDR + Autoruns.
Detect Rootkits with offline scans (GMER, chkrootkit, Volatility).
Rootkit fix = wipe & re-image, then rotate credentials.

mock.title: Q2 — Encryption for Email & Laptop Data-at-Rest
mock.context: The bank wants to implement encryption for both secure email communication and securing data at rest on laptops.

questions.q: (a) Explain the difference between symmetric and asymmetric encryption with real-life examples.
questions.a: Symmetric encryption uses one shared key to lock and unlock data — it's fast but both parties must somehow share that key safely (like one safe key both people own). Asymmetric encryption uses a key pair: a public key everyone can have and a private key kept secret (like a postbox — anyone can drop letters in, only you can open it).
points: Symmetric = one shared key (AES, 3DES). Fast.
Asymmetric = public + private key pair (RSA, ECC). Solves key sharing.
Symmetric analogy = safe key. Asymmetric = postbox.
Real systems combine both = hybrid encryption.
Example: HTTPS uses RSA to share an AES session key.

questions.q: (b) Compare AES and RSA in terms of performance, use cases, and security.
questions.a: AES is symmetric and very fast, so it's used for bulk data like disk encryption and database encryption. RSA is asymmetric and roughly 1000× slower, so it's only used for small jobs like key exchange and digital signatures. Both are secure today, but AES-256 is much more quantum-resistant than RSA.
points: AES = symmetric, 128/192/256-bit keys, very fast.
RSA = asymmetric, 2048+ bit keys, very slow.
AES used for files, disks, databases.
RSA used for key exchange and digital signatures.
AES is more quantum-resistant than RSA.

questions.q: (c) Evaluate when to use symmetric vs asymmetric encryption in a banking system.
questions.a: Use symmetric (AES) for big data — laptop full-disk encryption, customer database, backups and VPN traffic. Use asymmetric (RSA / ECC) for identity and trust — TLS website certificates, signing emails, and exchanging session keys. The best practice is hybrid: RSA to safely share an AES key, then AES for the heavy work.
points: Symmetric (AES) → bulk data: disks, DBs, backups, VPN payload.
Asymmetric (RSA/ECC) → identity, signatures, key exchange.
Always combine the two = hybrid encryption.
Rule: encrypt data with symmetric, encrypt the key with asymmetric.
Store master keys in an HSM, not on the same server as the data.

mock.title: Q3 — Firewall Strategy for HQ, ATMs and Web Servers
mock.context: The bank's IT manager is confused about which firewall technology to deploy across its headquarters, remote ATMs, and web servers.

questions.q: (a) Compare Packet Filtering, Stateful, and Next-Generation Firewalls with examples.
questions.a: A Packet Filter checks each packet alone using IP and port rules — fast but can be tricked. A Stateful Firewall tracks the whole connection in a state table, so it knows which return packets are valid. A Next-Generation Firewall (NGFW) does all that plus deep packet inspection, IPS, app awareness, user identity and TLS inspection.
points: Packet Filter = stateless, L3/L4, fast but weak.
Stateful = tracks connections, blocks unsolicited traffic.
NGFW = stateful + DPI + IPS + app + identity awareness.
PF example = router ACL. Stateful = ASA. NGFW = Palo Alto.
Cost & power: PF < Stateful < NGFW.

questions.q: (b) Recommend a firewall architecture for internal banking systems and public web services.
questions.a: Use a Screened Subnet (DMZ) design with two NGFWs in HA pairs. The outer NGFW protects the public web and email servers in the DMZ; the inner NGFW separates the DMZ from the internal core banking network. ATMs connect over IPsec VPN, and remote staff use SSL VPN with MFA.
points: Two NGFWs in HA pairs (different vendors if possible).
Outer NGFW + DMZ for web/email/public APIs.
Inner NGFW protects core banking systems.
ATMs → site-to-site IPsec VPN.
Remote staff → SSL VPN with certificates + MFA.

questions.q: (c) Limitations of firewalls and how a Distributed Firewall Architecture helps.
questions.a: Firewalls only guard the network edge — once an attacker is inside (via phishing, USB, insider) they can move freely. They also can't easily inspect encrypted traffic. A Distributed Firewall puts a small enforcement point on every server, laptop and VM with one central policy, so attackers can't move sideways even after a breach.
points: Firewalls don't stop insider threats or phishing.
Limited visibility into encrypted and east-west traffic.
Distributed FW = enforcement on every host/VM, central policy.
Stops lateral movement after a breach.
Tools: Windows Defender Firewall + GPO, NSX, Illumio, AWS/Azure security groups.

mock.title: Q4 — SSL VPN, X.509 Certificates and Trust Errors
mock.context: Bank staff working remotely are required to connect securely to the central server. A few employees report seeing 'certificate not trusted' errors during login.

questions.q: (a) Explain how an SSL VPN works with X.509 certificates.
questions.a: An SSL VPN builds an encrypted TLS tunnel over port 443 between the user and the bank's gateway. The gateway has an X.509 certificate signed by a trusted CA, which proves the gateway's identity. After the client checks the certificate, both sides agree on a symmetric AES session key and all VPN traffic is encrypted with it.
points: SSL VPN = TLS tunnel on TCP/443 (firewall-friendly).
Trust comes from an X.509 cert signed by a CA.
TLS handshake → exchange keys → derive AES session key.
Mutual TLS proves both server AND client identity.
Bulk traffic encrypted with AES-GCM.

questions.q: (b) Describe how a client verifies a server certificate (and why users see 'certificate not trusted').
questions.a: The client checks: (1) the cert chain leads to a CA in its trust store, (2) the signature is valid, (3) the cert is not expired, (4) the hostname matches, and (5) the cert isn't revoked (CRL/OCSP). If any check fails the user sees 'certificate not trusted'. The most common bank cause is the internal root CA not being installed on the laptop.
points: Checks: chain of trust, signature, dates, hostname, revocation.
Trust root must exist on the client.
Common error causes: missing root CA, expired cert, wrong clock, wrong hostname.
Use ECDHE for forward secrecy.
Fix = deploy internal root CA to laptops via GPO.

questions.q: (c) Compare SSL VPN, OpenVPN, and L2TP/IPsec VPN.
questions.a: SSL VPN (e.g. Cisco AnyConnect) uses TLS on port 443, so it works through almost any firewall and is easy for staff. OpenVPN is open-source TLS VPN that runs on UDP or TCP — strong, flexible and fast. L2TP/IPsec is built into most operating systems but uses uncommon ports (UDP 500/4500) that hotels often block.
points: SSL VPN: TCP/443, easy through firewalls, vendor clients.
OpenVPN: open-source TLS, very flexible, fast over UDP.
L2TP/IPsec: built-in on Windows/macOS/iOS, often blocked on public Wi-Fi.
All three are secure if configured properly.
Best for travelling staff = SSL VPN or OpenVPN over 443.

mock.title: Q5 — Lost PGP Keys at the Bank
mock.context: The bank uses PGP/GPG for signing emails and encrypting sensitive documents. After 6 months, staff complain they're unable to decrypt files due to lost keys.

questions.q: (a) How does GPG4WIN / GPG (Mac) manage public-private key pairs?
questions.a: GPG creates an asymmetric key pair (e.g. RSA-4096 or Ed25519) made of a public key (shared with others) and a private key (kept secret and protected by a passphrase). To encrypt, GPG uses the recipient's public key on a random AES session key (hybrid). To sign, GPG hashes the message and encrypts the hash with the sender's private key. Kleopatra is the GUI used to manage all of this.
points: Key pair = primary key + capability subkeys (sign / encrypt).
Private key encrypted with passphrase, stored locally.
Encryption is hybrid: AES session key + recipient's public key.
Signing = hash + encrypt with sender's private key.
Always generate and back up a Revocation Certificate.

questions.q: (b) Key components of a PGP keyring and their use in secure communication.
questions.a: A keyring stores all the keys a user works with. It has a public keyring (other people's public keys) and a private keyring (the user's own secret keys). Each entry contains a primary key, subkeys, user IDs, signatures, a fingerprint and a trust level. Fingerprints should be checked out-of-band before trusting a key.
points: Public keyring + private keyring.
Components: primary key, subkeys, UIDs, signatures, fingerprint, trust DB.
Subkeys split capabilities (sign vs encrypt).
Trust = Web of Trust or internal CA-style signing.
Verify the full fingerprint out-of-band before trusting a key.

questions.q: (c) Risks of no key management policy + best practices for key lifecycle in banks.
questions.a: Without a policy the bank risks lost keys (data unrecoverable), stolen keys (data leaked), impersonation, and compliance failures (GDPR, PCI-DSS). The fix is a full key lifecycle: Generate → Distribute → Store → Use → Rotate → Revoke → Archive → Destroy. Use HSMs / hardware tokens, escrow encryption keys (never signing keys) and revoke immediately on staff exit.
points: Risks: data loss, leaks, impersonation, compliance fines.
Lifecycle: G-D-S-U-R-R-A-D.
Store private keys in HSM or hardware tokens (YubiKey).
Escrow encryption keys, NEVER signing keys.
Rotate on schedule, revoke instantly on staff departure.
